subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Papers, boards, timbers, metals and polymers

questions.q: In what unit is the weight of paper and board measured?
questions.explain: Paper and board weight (and thus thickness/quality) is specified in grams per square metre, or gsm.

questions.q: Why does corrugated card contain a fluted (wavy) layer between two flat liners?
options: To add strength and impact protection while staying lightweight
To allow it to be printed on both sides
To make it conduct heat away from contents
questions.explain: The fluted middle layer resists crushing and cushions impacts, giving strength without much added weight.

questions.q: Hardwoods are obtained from which type of tree?
questions.explain: Hardwoods come from broadleaved deciduous trees, while softwoods come from coniferous trees.

questions.q: Which of the following is a softwood?
questions.explain: Pine is a coniferous softwood; oak, mahogany and beech are all hardwoods.

questions.q: A designer needs a low-cost board that machines cleanly, has no grain and gives a smooth surface for painting. Which is the best choice?
questions.explain: MDF is an inexpensive manufactured board with a smooth, grain-free surface ideal for machining and painting.

questions.q: What defines a ferrous metal?
options: It is always an alloy of copper
questions.explain: Ferrous metals contain iron, which makes most of them magnetic and prone to rusting.

questions.q: Brass is an alloy made mainly from which two metals?
questions.explain: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; copper and tin instead make bronze.

questions.q: What is the key characteristic of a thermoforming (thermoplastic) polymer?
options: It can be reheated and reshaped repeatedly
It sets permanently and cannot be remoulded
It is always a natural material
questions.explain: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped many times, unlike thermosetting polymers.

questions.q: Which of the following is a thermosetting polymer?
questions.explain: Melamine formaldehyde is a thermoset that sets permanently; the others are thermoplastics.

questions.q: A student needs a rigid, transparent polymer that can be line-bent into a display stand. Which is most suitable?
questions.explain: Acrylic is a rigid, transparent thermoplastic that softens for line-bending, making it ideal for display stands.

questions.q: Which of these is a natural fibre obtained from a plant?
questions.explain: Cotton is a natural plant fibre; polyester, nylon and elastane are synthetic fibres made from oil.

questions.q: Wool is a natural fibre that comes from which source?
questions.explain: Wool is an animal-based natural fibre, most commonly from sheep.

questions.q: Polyester is classed as a synthetic fibre because it is:
questions.explain: Synthetic fibres such as polyester are made from petrochemicals derived from crude oil.

questions.q: A shirt is made from polycotton (a polyester and cotton blend). What is the main benefit of blending these fibres?
options: It combines cotton's comfort with polyester's strength and crease resistance
It makes the fabric fully waterproof
It removes the need for any dyeing
It makes the fabric electrically conductive
questions.explain: Blending gives the softness and absorbency of cotton with the durability and crease resistance of polyester.

questions.q: How is a woven fabric constructed?
options: By interlacing warp and weft threads at right angles
By interlocking loops of a single yarn
By bonding fibres together with heat or glue
By pouring liquid polymer into a mould
questions.explain: Woven fabrics are made by interlacing lengthwise warp threads with crosswise weft threads.

questions.q: What does the working property 'malleability' describe?
options: The ability to be permanently deformed or shaped without cracking
The ability to return to its original shape after stretching
The ability to soak up moisture
The ability to melt when heated
questions.explain: Malleability is the ability of a material to be pressed, hammered or rolled into shape without cracking.

questions.q: A material with high ductility can best be:
options: Drawn out into a thin wire
questions.explain: Ductility is the ability to be stretched or drawn into wires without breaking, as with copper.

questions.q: The working property 'hardness' is defined as a material's resistance to:
questions.explain: Hardness is a material's ability to resist scratching, wear and abrasion.

questions.q: Which property describes a material's ability to absorb impact or shock without fracturing?
questions.explain: Toughness is the ability to withstand sudden impact or shock loads without breaking, the opposite of brittleness.

questions.q: A component must not sag or break when a heavy load pulls on it. Which property is most important?
questions.explain: Tensile strength is resistance to being pulled apart, which matters most when a material is under a pulling (tension) load.
